lesson_title: The Tuckshop, the Choir and the Leaking Tank
hook_text: Your school at first break is a perfect map of South Africa. Watch.
clip_script: The bell rings for first break, and in two minutes the school has arranged itself: a crush at the tuckshop, comfortable groups in the quad, nobody on the far field. Nobody planned it — everyone just moved toward what they wanted. Congratulations: you now understand population distribution. Scale it up. South Africa's tuckshop is Gauteng — the smallest province holding a quarter of the country, because that's where work has been served since gold was struck in 1886. The far field is the Northern Cape: the biggest province, about two people per square kilometre, because no rain means no farms means no jobs. Now the counting: density is people divided by space — three million people on twenty-five thousand square kilometres is one hundred and twenty per square kilometre. But careful — density is an average, and averages hide the crush. Say the school averages three learners per classroom of space and you've missed the forty fighting at the tuckshop counter. And here's the dark twist the full lesson unpacks: when people crowd to the city's tuckshop and find no housing, they settle on the land nobody claimed — and unclaimed city land is so often the floodplain. Where the people, the land and the water meet — that's where geography stops being theory.
visual_style: Overhead time-lapse of a schoolyard filling at break, morphing into a population dot-map of South Africa; a density division animating on screen; final beat of a river rising toward homes at its bank.
pacing: Fast schoolyard open, the Gauteng and Northern Cape beats land the map, the average trap surprises, the floodplain twist lingers.
call_to_action: Watch the full revision session to connect people, pyramids and water.
